questions.question: Which of the following best describes binary search?

options.A: An algorithm that checks each element one by one from the beginning
options.B: An algorithm that starts at the middle of a sorted data set and eliminates half the data each step
options.C: An algorithm that sorts a list before searching it
options.D: An algorithm that divides data into groups and searches each group in parallel

questions.explanation: The binary search algorithm starts at the middle of a sorted data set and eliminates half of the data. This repeats until the desired value is found or all elements have been eliminated.

questions.question: A programmer needs to search for a value in an unsorted list of 1,000 elements. Which of the following correctly describes which search algorithm can be used?

options.A: Binary search only, because it is the most efficient
options.B: Linear search only, because binary search requires sorted data
options.C: Either binary or linear search because both work on unsorted data
options.D: Neither because the list is too large

questions.explanation: Data must be in sorted order to use binary search. Linear search checks each element in order and works on any list. For an unsorted list, only linear search can be used without first sorting.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes procedural abstraction?

options.A: The process of converting a program from one language to another
options.B: A common type of abstraction that provides a name for a process and allows a procedure to be used knowing only what it does, not how it does it
options.C: The process of removing all variables and replacing them with constants
options.D: A method of compressing code to reduce the number of lines

questions.explanation: Procedural abstraction provides a name for a process and allows a procedure to be used only knowing what it does, not how it does it. This hides implementation details from the user of the procedure.

questions.question: A software library contains a procedure called sortList. A programmer uses it to sort data without knowing exactly how it works internally. Which of the following best describes what this demonstrates?

options.A: Data abstraction — the list is being treated as a single value
options.B: Procedural abstraction — the programmer uses the procedure knowing only what it does, not how
options.C: Iteration — the sorting involves repeating comparisons
options.D: Modularity — the sorting is done in a separate program

questions.explanation: Procedural abstraction provides a name for a process and allows a procedure to be used only knowing what it does, not how it does it. Using sortList without knowing its implementation is procedural abstraction.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a simulation?

options.A: A program that displays real-time data from sensors
options.B: An abstraction of a more complex object or phenomenon for a specific purpose
options.C: A program that stores and retrieves data from a database
options.D: An algorithm that solves a problem in the most efficient way

questions.explanation: Simulations are abstractions of more complex objects or phenomena for a specific purpose. They use varying sets of values to reflect the changing state of a phenomenon.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes algorithmic efficiency?

options.A: How accurately an algorithm produces correct output
options.B: An estimation of the amount of computational resources used by an algorithm
options.C: The number of lines of code in an algorithm
options.D: How readable and well-documented an algorithm is

questions.explanation: Algorithmic efficiency is an estimation of the amount of computational resources used by an algorithm. It is typically expressed as a function of the size of the input.

questions.question: Which of the following types of algorithmic efficiency is considered UNREASONABLE?

options.A: Linear efficiency
options.B: Quadratic efficiency
options.C: Cubic efficiency
options.D: Exponential efficiency

questions.explanation: Exponential efficiency is considered unreasonable. Reasonable efficiency includes polynomial types (constant, linear, square, cube, etc.). Exponential and factorial efficiency are unreasonable because they grow too quickly for large inputs.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a decidable problem?

options.A: A problem that can be solved in polynomial time
options.B: A decision problem for which an algorithm can be written that always produces a correct yes or no answer for all inputs
options.C: A problem that has exactly one correct solution
options.D: A problem that can be solved using a heuristic approach

questions.explanation: A decidable problem is a decision problem for which an algorithm can be written that is always capable of producing a correct yes or no answer.

questions.stimulus:
There are 32 students standing in a classroom. Two different algorithms are given for finding the average height.

Algorithm A:
Step 1: All students stand.
Step 2: A randomly selected student writes their height on a card and is seated.
Step 3: A randomly selected standing student adds their height to the value on the card, records the new value, and is seated.
Step 4: Repeat step 3 until no students remain.
Step 5: Divide the sum by 32.

Algorithm B:
Step 1: All students stand.
Step 2: Each student is given a card and writes their height.
Step 3: Standing students form random pairs. Each pair adds their numbers and writes the result on one card; the other student is seated.
Step 4: Repeat step 3 until one student remains.
Step 5: Divide the final sum by 32.
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true?

options.A: Algorithm A always calculates the correct average, but Algorithm B does not
options.B: Algorithm B always calculates the correct average, but Algorithm A does not
options.C: Both Algorithm A and Algorithm B always calculate the correct average
options.D: Neither Algorithm A nor Algorithm B calculates the correct average

questions.explanation: Both algorithms correctly compute the sum of all heights and divide by 32 — they just do so in different orders. Algorithm B is more parallel (pairs add simultaneously) while Algorithm A is sequential. Algorithms can be written in different ways and still accomplish the same task.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the three building blocks that can be used to construct any algorithm?

options.A: Variables, procedures, and lists
options.B: Sequencing, selection, and iteration
options.C: Addition, subtraction, and comparison

questions.explanation: Every algorithm can be constructed using combinations of sequencing, selection, and iteration. These three building blocks are sufficient to express any algorithm.

questions.question: A programmer writes an algorithm using natural language as numbered steps. Another programmer rewrites it in pseudocode. Which of the following best describes the relationship between these two representations?

questions.explanation: Beyond visual and textual programming languages, algorithms can be expressed in a variety of ways such as natural language, diagrams, and pseudocode. Both representations can describe the same algorithm.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how new algorithms can be created?

options.B: Algorithms can be created from an idea, by combining existing algorithms, or by modifying existing algorithms
options.C: New algorithms must always be derived from existing ones
options.D: Algorithms are fixed and cannot be modified once created

questions.explanation: Algorithms can be created from an idea, by combining existing algorithms, or by modifying existing algorithms. Knowledge of existing algorithms can help in constructing new ones.

questions.question: What is a heuristic approach to a problem?

options.B: An approach that produces a solution not guaranteed to be optimal but used when finding an optimal solution is impractical
options.C: A mathematical proof that a problem cannot be solved
options.D: An approach that converts an undecidable problem into a decidable one

questions.explanation: A heuristic approach produces a solution that is not guaranteed to be optimal but may be used when techniques guaranteed to find an optimal solution are impractical due to unreasonable running time.

options.B: Speedup ≈ 1.6
options.C: Speedup = 2
options.D: Speedup = 3

questions.explanation: Sequential time: 10+40+25+35+5 = 115 seconds. Parallel time: sequential tasks (10+5=15) + longest parallel task (40) = 55 seconds. Speedup = 115/55 ≈ 2.09. questions.question: The Halting Problem asks whether a given program will eventually stop running. This is a famous example of an undecidable problem. Which of the following best describes what this means?

questions.explanation: Using procedural abstraction allows programmers to change the internals of a procedure without notifying users as long as what the procedure does is preserved.

questions.question: A student argues that undecidable problems will be solvable once quantum computers are powerful enough. Which of the following best evaluates this argument?

options.A: The student is correct — quantum computers can solve problems classical computers cannot
options.B: The student is incorrect — undecidability is a mathematical property meaning no algorithm can exist, regardless of computing power or type
options.C: The student is correct — quantum computers have already solved some undecidable problems
options.D: The student is partially correct — quantum computers can solve undecidable problems given enough time

questions.explanation: Undecidability is not about computing power — it is a mathematical property proven to mean that no algorithm on any type of computer can always produce a correct answer. More powerful computers cannot overcome fundamental mathematical impossibility.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes a complete traversal of a list versus a partial traversal?

options.A: A complete traversal accesses only the first and last elements; a partial traversal accesses all elements
options.B: A complete traversal accesses every element in the list; a partial traversal accesses only some elements

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the difference between a decision problem and an optimization problem?

options.A: Decision problems are harder than optimization problems
options.B: A decision problem has a yes/no answer while an optimization problem seeks to find the best solution
options.C: Optimization problems always have reasonable running time while decision problems do not
options.D: Decision problems can only be solved by humans

questions.explanation: A decision problem is one with a yes or no answer. An optimization problem has the goal of finding the best solution. For example, 'Is there a path from A to B?' is a decision problem; 'What is the shortest path?' is an optimization problem.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are true about REPEAT UNTIL(condition) loops?

options.A: If the condition is true before the loop starts, the loop body executes at least once
options.B: If the condition is true before the loop starts, the loop body is not executed at all
options.C: An infinite loop occurs when the ending condition never evaluates to true
options.D: REPEAT UNTIL always executes the loop body at least once

questions.explanation: In REPEAT UNTIL, if the condition is true initially the loop body does not execute at all (B). An infinite loop occurs when the ending condition never becomes true (C). The condition is checked before execution so if true initially the body never runs (A and D are false).

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are classified as REASONABLE running times?

options.A: Linear efficiency (n steps)
options.B: Exponential efficiency (2ⁿ steps)
options.C: Quadratic efficiency (n² steps)
options.D: Factorial efficiency (n! steps)

questions.explanation: Reasonable running times include polynomial efficiency or lower: constant, linear (n), quadratic (n²), cubic (n³), etc. Exponential (2ⁿ) and factorial (n!) are unreasonable because they grow too quickly for large inputs.

questions.stimulus: A programmer has a sorted list of 1,000 student ID numbers and needs to determine whether a specific ID is in the list.
questions.question:

Part B: Describe what the binary search algorithm does step by step.

Part C: The programmer later receives an unsorted list of 500 additional IDs to search through. Explain whether binary search can be used on this new list without modification and what would need to happen first.
questions.rubric:
PART A (2 points):
Award 1 point for identifying binary search as more efficient.
Award 1 point for explaining: binary search eliminates half the remaining data with each step, making it much faster than linear search which checks elements one at a time on large sorted data sets.

PART B (2 points):
Award 1 point for: binary search starts at the middle of the sorted data set and checks if the target is equal to, less than, or greater than the middle element.
Award 1 point for: based on the comparison, half the data is eliminated and the process repeats on the remaining half until the value is found or all elements are eliminated.

PART C (2 points):
Award 1 point for explaining that binary search cannot be used directly on an unsorted list — data must be in sorted order.
Award 1 point for explaining what must happen first: the list must be sorted before binary search can be applied.
